questions.stem: In this core practical, what is the independent variable?

options.text: the absorber material between source and detector
options.explanation: The absorber is deliberately changed to test penetration.
Count rate is measured, so it is the dependent variable.
Distance is held fixed — a control variable.
Temperature is irrelevant here.

questions.stem: Which quantity is the dependent variable?

options.explanation: Not a variable of this experiment.
The count rate responds to the absorber change.
Absorbers are chosen by the experimenter.
The source is controlled, not measured.

questions.stem: Why is the source kept at a fixed distance from the tube?

options.text: because the tube only works at 3 cm
options.explanation: The tube works at any reasonable distance.
Absorber use is unrelated to distance.

options.text: so that count-rate changes can only be due to the absorber
options.explanation: Holding geometry constant isolates the absorber’s effect.

options.text: to make the source decay faster
options.explanation: Distance does not change decay behaviour.

questions.stem: Which absorber set matches the investigation?

options.explanation: Water is not part of this absorber set.
Aluminium alone cannot separate all three radiations.
Colour is irrelevant; material and thickness matter.

options.text: paper, aluminium of several thicknesses, lead
options.explanation: The three absorbers separate alpha, beta and gamma.

questions.stem: Sources are stored in lead-lined containers when not in use because…

options.text: lead shielding keeps emissions contained between measurements
options.explanation: Storage shielding protects people when no measurement is running.

options.text: lead makes the source more active
options.explanation: Shielding never changes the source’s activity.
Nothing stops radioactive decay.

options.text: the counter needs lead to work
options.explanation: The counter is independent of storage shielding.

questions.stem: Name the instrument used to measure the count rate in this experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: A Geiger-Müller tube connected to a counter measures the count rate.

questions.stem: State one control variable and one safety precaution for this experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: Control: keep the same source (or the same source-to-tube distance, or the same location). Safety: handle sources with tongs and store them in lead-lined containers.

questions.stem: Explain why readings are repeated and averaged in this investigation.
questions.modelAnswer: Radioactive decay is random, so single readings fluctuate; repeating each measurement and averaging reduces the effect of those fluctuations.

questions.stem: A student measures with no absorber, then paper, then aluminium. The count rates are 850, 848 and 210. What does this suggest about the emission, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Paper leaves the rate almost unchanged (850 → 848), so alpha is absent; aluminium cuts it sharply (848 → 210), so beta is being absorbed — the source emits beta.

questions.stem: Why is the background count measured before any source is used?

options.text: to make the source decay slower
options.explanation: Nothing about the source changes.

options.text: to subtract it from later readings for corrected count rates
options.explanation: Background subtraction isolates the source’s contribution.

options.text: to check the source is working
options.explanation: The source is not present during the background measurement.
Absorbers need no calibration by background.

questions.stem: The corrected count rate falls to background level behind paper. Which radiation was emitted?

options.explanation: Gamma penetrates paper easily.
The drop to background shows radiation was present and then absorbed.
Only alpha is stopped by paper.
Beta penetrates paper.

questions.stem: After a few millimetres of lead, some counts above background remain. What does that indicate?

options.explanation: Irradiation does not make the lead a source.
Residual gamma, not fault, explains the counts.
Alpha cannot pass anything, let alone lead.

options.text: a gamma component is still penetrating
options.explanation: Only gamma survives modest lead shielding.

questions.stem: What does a corrected count rate close to zero tell you about the absorber used?

options.text: it fully absorbed the emitted radiation
options.explanation: Counts at background mean the source contributes nothing through that absorber.

options.text: the absorber emits its own radiation
options.explanation: Absorbers do not emit.

options.text: the source has decayed away completely
options.explanation: Decay takes far longer than a measurement session.
The comparison itself is the method working as intended.

questions.stem: A source shows a drop at paper AND a further drop at aluminium, with a residual behind lead. What is emitted?

options.explanation: Gamma alone would show no paper or aluminium step.

options.text: alpha and beta, with some gamma
options.explanation: Two absorption steps identify two components; the lead residual adds gamma.
Alpha alone would show only the paper drop.
Beta alone would pass paper unchanged.

questions.stem: Describe how to measure the background count rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Record the count for one minute with no source present, repeat and average; the result is the background count rate to subtract later.

questions.stem: State what count-rate change reveals a beta emitter in this experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: A sharp fall in corrected count rate when a few millimetres of aluminium are inserted identifies beta emission.

questions.stem: Explain why the absorbers are tested one at a time rather than all together.
questions.modelAnswer: Stacking absorbers would hide which one caused the change; testing one at a time attributes each count-rate drop to a single absorber, so each radiation is identified cleanly.

questions.stem: Corrected rates are: no absorber 600, paper 595, aluminium 60, lead 55. Identify the emission(s) and state what the lead residual shows.
questions.modelAnswer: Paper changes nothing (no alpha); aluminium drops the rate to near background (beta present); the small lead residual of 55 suggests a weak gamma component above background.

questions.stem: Which is a systematic error to avoid in this experiment?

options.explanation: Absorber choice is the design, not an error.
Averaging reduces error; it is not an error.

options.text: a spare source sitting near the counter
options.explanation: A stray source lifts every reading the same way.
Single high counts are random fluctuation.

questions.stem: Why should every run take place in the same location?

options.text: the tube only works in one place
options.explanation: The tube works anywhere.
Location does not change decay.

options.text: absorbers work differently in different rooms
options.explanation: Absorption physics is location-independent.

options.text: background radiation varies from place to place
options.explanation: Moving changes the baseline being subtracted.

questions.stem: Why is a source with a long half-life preferred here?

options.text: its activity stays steady during the whole experiment
options.explanation: A fading source would corrupt comparisons between absorbers.
Long half-life does not imply low danger.
Cost is not the stated reason.
Half-life says nothing about the radiation type.

questions.stem: Which practice best reduces exposure while a source is in use?

options.text: warm it to room temperature first
options.explanation: Temperature is irrelevant.

options.text: keep it at arm’s length with tongs for the shortest time needed
options.explanation: Distance plus tongs plus minimal time is the standard trio.

options.text: hold it close to keep control of it
options.explanation: Closeness increases dose.

options.text: look directly at it to monitor it
options.explanation: Looking has no effect and eye exposure matters.

questions.stem: A student leaves the source on the bench next to the tube for ten minutes between runs. What effect does this have?

options.text: only the first reading is affected
options.explanation: The bias persists while the source sits there.

options.text: the source decays twice as fast
options.explanation: Decay rate is unaffected by position.

options.text: every subsequent reading is biased upward
options.explanation: The nearby source adds counts to all later measurements — systematic.

options.text: no effect, storage position does not matter
options.explanation: Storage position absolutely matters.

questions.stem: State three safety precautions for handling a radioactive source.
questions.modelAnswer: Keep the source in a lead-lined container when not in use, handle it with tongs, and stay at a good distance while minimising the time it is out.

questions.stem: Distinguish a systematic error from a random error in this experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: A systematic error shifts all readings the same way (such as a stray source nearby), while a random error scatters readings unpredictably (such as counting noise from decay randomness).

questions.stem: Explain why tongs, rather than gloves alone, are used to move the source.
questions.modelAnswer: Tongs hold the source at a distance, and dose falls sharply with separation; gloves alone would keep the source against the hand at zero distance.

questions.stem: During the experiment the lab’s background rises because a colleague unboxes a different source across the room. Explain the effect on your corrected rates and one fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The raised background is still subtracted if re-measured, but a fixed old subtraction over-corrects or under-corrects every rate; the fix is to re-measure the background in the changed conditions (and keep all sources far from the counter).
